subject: ela
intro: Each item gives you two texts in different forms, such as a poem and a story passage. Both texts explore the same theme or topic. Read both, then answer the question. Everything you need is in the item.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
The seed lies still beneath the snow,
It waits, it waits, it does not show.
But spring will come, the sun will call,
And up it climbs above them all.

STORY:
Maya planted the bean on a cold March morning and worried it would never grow. Every day she checked the bare pot and saw only brown soil. Her brother laughed and said she had wasted the seed. Maya kept watering it anyway, even when nothing changed. One warm afternoon in April, she found a tiny green shoot pushing up through the dirt. She had been right to wait.

What shared theme do both the poem and the story explore?
items.answer: Both texts explore the theme that patience and waiting are rewarded, because good things take time to grow.

steps: Find what the poem is about: a seed waits quietly under the snow and finally grows in spring.
Find what the story is about: Maya waters a bean and waits patiently until a green shoot finally appears.
Look for the idea both share, not just the topic of plants. In both, waiting patiently leads to growth.
State the shared theme: patience and waiting are rewarded because good things take time.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below.

TEXT 1 (a poem):
The storm may shake the oak tree's crown,
But deep below it holds its ground.
The wind can howl, the branches sway,
The rooted oak will stay, will stay.

TEXT 2 (a story passage):
When the floodwaters rose, the Ramos family lost their fence and their garden, but they did not leave. Mr. Ramos said the house had stood for sixty years and would stand again. They cleaned the mud, fixed the broken steps, and stayed in their town. By summer, the garden bloomed once more.

Which form is Text 1, and which form is Text 2?
items.answer: Text 1 is a poem, and Text 2 is a story passage (prose).

steps: Look at Text 1: it has short lines that break before the edge of the page and a rhythm, which are features of a poem.
Notice the rhymes in Text 1: crown and ground, sway and stay. Rhyme is a common feature of poems.
Look at Text 2: it is written in full sentences and paragraphs that tell events in order, which is the form of a story passage (prose).
Match each form: Text 1 is a poem, Text 2 is a story passage.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
A new kid stands beside the door,
He does not know the room before.
But one kind word, one open chair,
Can turn cold air to friendly air.

STORY:
Devon was the new student, and on his first day he sat alone at lunch, staring at his tray. The cafeteria felt enormous and loud. Then a girl named Priya slid her tray across from his and asked if he liked comic books. By the end of lunch they were trading drawings, and Devon felt, for the first time, that he might belong here.

What topic do both the poem and the story focus on?
items.answer: Both texts focus on being the new kid and how a small act of kindness helps a newcomer feel welcome.

steps: Identify the poem's focus: a new kid stands alone until a kind word makes the room feel friendly.
Identify the story's focus: Devon is the new student sitting alone until Priya is kind and he feels he belongs.
Find the shared topic: both center on a newcomer and the kindness that helps them feel welcome.
State the shared topic: being the new kid and how kindness makes a newcomer feel they belong.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below. They are in different forms.

TEXT A (a poem):
The little boat fought wave on wave,
Its captain small but very brave.
Though fear was loud, she steered ahead,
And reached the shore the doubters dread.

TEXT B (a story passage):
The rowboat tipped in the rough water, and Lena's arms ached, but she did not stop rowing. The other campers on shore had said she could never make it across the lake alone. Lena fixed her eyes on the dock and pulled the oars again and again. When the boat finally bumped the wooden dock, she let out a long, proud breath.

Which text uses short rhyming lines, and which text uses sentences that tell events one after another?
items.answer: Text A (the poem) uses short rhyming lines. Text B (the story passage) uses sentences that tell events one after another.

steps: Look at Text A: it is built from short lines that rhyme (wave and brave, ahead and dread), which is the form of a poem.
Look at Text B: it is built from full sentences in a paragraph that tell what happens step by step, which is the form of a story.
Match the feature to the text: short rhyming lines belong to Text A, and event-by-event sentences belong to Text B.
Be careful not to swap them: the poem does not tell a long plot, and the story does not rhyme.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
He missed the goal, he missed the shot,
He wanted to give up, he thought.
But still he ran back to the line,
To try again, and try, and shine.

STORY:
Rosa failed her spelling test on Monday and felt like quitting the class spelling bee. She almost crumpled her word list and threw it away. Instead, she taped it to her wall and studied a little each night. The next Friday, she spelled every word correctly. Trying again had made all the difference.

What shared theme do both texts explore?
items.answer: Both texts explore the theme that you should not give up; trying again after failing leads to success.

steps: Read the poem: a player misses and wants to quit but goes back to try again.
Read the story: Rosa fails a test and almost quits but studies and tries again, then succeeds.
Look past the topics (sports, spelling) to the idea both share.
State the shared theme: do not give up, because trying again after failure leads to success.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below.

TEXT 1 (a poem):
The river never stops to rest,
It curves and turns and does its best.
It does not race, it does not fight,
It simply flows from morn to night.

TEXT 2 (a story passage):
Grandpa told Sam that he had worked at the same bakery for forty years. Some days were slow and some were busy, but he showed up every morning and made the bread. He never rushed and never quit. Sam looked at the steady old hands kneading the dough and understood what his grandpa was trying to teach him.

Both texts admire the same quality. Which quality do they both admire?
items.answer: Both texts admire steadiness, the value of moving forward calmly and not quitting, day after day.

steps: Notice what the poem praises: a river that never stops, never races, and simply keeps flowing.
Notice what the story praises: Grandpa who shows up every morning for forty years, never rushing and never quitting.
Find the shared quality both admire: steady, calm persistence over time.
State it: both admire steadiness, moving forward calmly and not quitting.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
The lantern glows when night is near,
It turns the darkness less to fear.
A single light, though small and thin,
Can help a tired traveler in.

STORY:
When the power went out during the storm, the whole street fell dark and quiet. Mrs. Okafor set a candle in her front window so her neighbors could find their way to her porch. One by one, people gathered there, sharing blankets and stories until the lights came back. The small flame had brought them together.

What topic do both texts share?
items.answer: Both texts share the topic of a small light bringing comfort and help to people in the dark.

steps: Identify the poem's subject: a lantern that makes the dark less scary and helps a tired traveler.
Identify the story's subject: a candle Mrs. Okafor places in the window that guides and comforts her neighbors.
Find the shared topic: a small light offering comfort and help to people in darkness.
State the shared topic: a small light bringing comfort and help to people in the dark.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below. They are written in different forms.

TEXT A (a poem):
My sister tugs the kite string tight,
She lifts it up with all her might.
The wind takes hold, the kite climbs high,
We cheer to see it touch the sky.

TEXT B (a story passage):
The Carter twins spent all Saturday building a model rocket in the garage. They glued the fins, painted the body, and argued about the best place to launch it. When it finally shot into the air over the empty field, they jumped and shouted together, proud of what they had made.

Which text is a poem, and which text is a story passage?
items.answer: Text A is a poem, and Text B is a story passage (prose).

steps: Look at Text A: it has short lines that break early and rhyme (tight and might, high and sky), which marks it as a poem.
Look at Text B: it is a paragraph of full sentences telling events in order, which marks it as a story passage.
Match each: Text A is the poem, Text B is the story.
Do not swap them; the poem is the rhyming short-line text, not the paragraph.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
The winter comes, the leaves all fall,
The tree stands bare and gray and tall.
But hidden buds wait through the cold,
For spring to come and turn them gold.

STORY:
After his dog died, Eli did not want to play outside or talk to his friends. The days felt empty and slow. His mom told him that sadness, like winter, does not last forever. Slowly, week by week, Eli began to laugh again and even adopted a kitten. The heavy feeling had finally lifted.

What shared theme do both texts explore about hard times?
items.answer: Both texts explore the theme that hard, sad times do not last forever; better times come again, just as spring follows winter.

steps: Read the poem: winter makes the tree bare, but hidden buds wait for spring to return.
Read the story: Eli is sad after his dog dies, but the sadness lifts and he laughs again.
Connect the two: both use the idea that a hard season passes and good times return.
State the shared theme: hard, sad times do not last forever; better times come again.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below.

TEXT 1 (a poem):
She shares her lunch, she shares her seat,
She shares the shade in summer heat.
The more she gives, the more I see,
How kindness grows from you to me.

TEXT 2 (a story passage):
When the new family moved in next door with little furniture, the Nguyens brought over a hot meal and an extra chair. The next month, when the Nguyens' car broke down, that same family drove their kids to school for a week. Kindness, it seemed, kept coming back around the block.

Both texts share the same message about kindness. What is it?
items.answer: Both texts share the message that kindness spreads and comes back; when you give to others, kindness grows and returns.

steps: Read the poem: the more a person shares, the more kindness grows from one person to another.
Read the story: the Nguyens help a new family, and that family later helps them back.
Find the shared message: giving kindness causes more kindness to spread and return.
State it: kindness spreads and comes back when you give to others.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below. They are in different forms.

TEXT A (a poem):
The mountain looms, so steep, so wide,
He sets his pack and starts the climb.
One step, one breath, one foot, one stride,
He reaches the top in his own time.

TEXT B (a story passage):
The history report was twenty pages long, and Jamal had only a week to write it. At first the size of it scared him. So he split it into small parts and wrote one section each day. By Friday, the report was finished, page by page.

Which text uses short lines with a steady rhythm, and which text uses ordinary sentences in a paragraph?
items.answer: Text A (the poem) uses short lines with a steady rhythm. Text B (the story passage) uses ordinary sentences in a paragraph.

steps: Look at Text A: it is made of short lines with rhythm and rhyme (wide and stride, climb and time), the form of a poem.
Look at Text B: it is made of ordinary full sentences grouped in a paragraph, the form of a story.
Match the feature to the right text: short rhythmic lines are Text A, paragraph sentences are Text B.
Avoid swapping: the poem is not the paragraph, and the story does not use rhyming short lines.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
The geese fly south in one long line,
No goose alone, but all combine.
They take their turns to lead the way,
And none gets lost, and none must stray.

STORY:
The soccer team had lost three games in a row by trying to score on their own. Then the coach taught them to pass and cover for each other on the field. Working together, they won their next match. No single player had carried the team; they had done it as one.

What shared theme do both texts explore?
items.answer: Both texts explore the theme that working together as a group is more successful than acting alone.

steps: Read the poem: geese fly in one line and take turns leading, so none gets lost.
Read the story: the team loses by playing alone, then wins by passing and working together.
Look for the shared idea behind both: success comes from cooperation, not from acting alone.
State the shared theme: working together as a group is more successful than acting alone.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below.

TEXT 1 (a poem):
The candle burns to give us light,
It melts itself to win the night.
It asks for nothing in return,
It only knows it wants to burn.

TEXT 2 (a story passage):
Grandma stayed up late every night sewing dresses so her children could go to school in clean clothes. She never bought new things for herself. Years later, when her daughter became a teacher, she finally understood all that her mother had quietly given up for her.

What topic do both texts share?
items.answer: Both texts share the topic of giving to others without expecting anything in return, a quiet kind of sacrifice.

steps: Identify the poem's subject: a candle that melts itself to give light and asks for nothing back.
Identify the story's subject: Grandma who gives up new things for herself so her children can go to school.
Find the shared topic: selfless giving, sacrificing for others without expecting a reward.
State it: giving to others without expecting anything in return, a quiet sacrifice.

items.prompt:
Read the two texts below. They are written in different forms.

TEXT A (a poem):
The robin sings before the dawn,
While half the sleepy world yawns on.
It does not wait for light to start,
It sings the morning from its heart.

TEXT B (a story passage):
Every morning before school, Tomas got up while it was still dark to practice his violin. His family was still asleep, and the house was silent. He did not need anyone to remind him; he simply loved to play. By the time the sun rose, he had already filled the kitchen with music.

Which text is the poem, and which text is the story passage? Name one feature that tells you.
items.answer: Text A is the poem and Text B is the story passage. One feature: Text A is written in short rhyming lines, while Text B is written in full sentences in a paragraph that tell events.

steps: Look at Text A: it is built from short lines that rhyme (dawn and on, start and heart), a clear feature of a poem.
Look at Text B: it is built from full sentences in a paragraph that tell what Tomas does in order, a clear feature of a story.
Match each form: Text A is the poem, Text B is the story passage.
Name a feature: short rhyming lines mark the poem, while event-telling sentences in a paragraph mark the story.

items.prompt:
Read the poem and the story passage below.

POEM:
The old clock ticks the same each day,
Through sun and storm it keeps its way.
It does not stop, it does not pause,
It marks the time without a cause.

STORY:
No matter what happened, Aunt Rita opened her little shop at eight every morning. On snowy days, on her birthday, on the day after her cat ran away, the lights came on and the door unlocked at eight. The whole neighborhood set their watches by her, trusting she would always be there.

What quality do both the clock in the poem and Aunt Rita in the story share?
items.answer: Both share the quality of dependability, being steady and reliable so others can count on them every day.

steps: Read the poem: the old clock keeps the same time every day through sun and storm and never stops.
Read the story: Aunt Rita opens her shop at eight every morning no matter what happens.
Find the shared quality: both are steady and can be relied on without fail.
State it: dependability, being reliable so others can count on them every day.
